Modern.brandNameRationale: Single word. Ship is the verb every modern product team lives by. The brand sits on the daily action of getting work in front of users. Plain, modern, immediately legible to anyone who has worked in software.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern SaaS has matured into a category with strong design conventions and a few dominant patterns. The customer is design-literate and impatient with anything that feels enterprise-stale. The opening is for a small product brand that talks like a product team and ships like one.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Linear (linear.app) holds the design-led product peer position. Notion (notion.so) sits in the workspace tier. Vercel (vercel.com) holds the developer-platform peer. Height (height.app) does the modern issue-tracking middle. We sit closest to Linear in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A product tool for teams that already ship and want a tool that doesn't slow them down.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Engineering managers, product managers, designers at companies of 20 to 500 people. Already use three SaaS tools and want the fourth to consolidate two of them.

dos: Show real screenshots, not stylized hero illustrations
Speak to the engineer who'd use the tool
Document the shortcuts on the page they appear

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Hartshorn is an old English place and surname with a quiet, slightly archaic register — the opposite of every modern SaaS naming convention. Software is the plain category word. The pair feels like a small firm that decided to opt out of the tech-naming arms race, and that decision is the brand.
Luxury.story: Hartshorn Software was founded by three engineers who had spent years inside larger software companies and wanted to build a smaller catalog of tools, more carefully. The company ships one major version per year. The team is intentionally small. The customers are loyal across decades.
Luxury.industrySummary: Most premium B2B software signals premium by being expensive. There's a smaller market for software that signals premium by being restrained, slow-roadmap, deeply documented, and built to last a decade. We belong there.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: JetBrains (jetbrains.com) holds the closest peer in seriousness and restraint. Panic (panic.com) sits in the craft-led peer position. Tinderbox (eastgate.com) does the heritage indie-software middle. We sit in their company.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small software house for teams that buy slowly and stay long.

targetAudience.primary: Senior engineering and product leaders at companies of 200 to 5000 engineers. They sign three-year contracts. They expect us to still be here in ten.

dos: Speak to the leader, not the analyst

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark with deliberate spacing. A small geometric mark, two perpendicular lines forming a quiet right angle, used as a hallmark on documentation, hardware, and the IDE plugin marketplace.

typography.rationale: A classical serif for the brand surface. A modern grotesk for the product surface. Each does its job and gets out of the way.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Docs is the most basic word for what a great deal of software is actually about: the document. The brand sits on the smallest unit of work, plain and unadorned.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most document and writing software is feature-heavy and slightly bloated. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the document, the cursor, and the page.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most writing tools fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some Japanese text-editor traditions and certain minimalist editors like iA Writer (ia.net) and Bear (bear.app).
Minimal.positioningStatement: A writing tool that does writing. That is the entire product.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who write daily and want a tool that gets out of the way. They distrust products that add features.

dos: Show the cursor and the page

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. DOCS in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, four letters with generous space. No icon. The app icon is the wordmark on a soft grey background. The website is the product.

typography.rationale: One face. The product is the cursor, the page, and the wordmark.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No AI features. No mood tracker. No collaboration sidebar. No newsletter. No notifications.

Corporate.tagline: Enterprise software for the modern operator.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Two words. Bayfield is a real place name with a quiet weight; it sounds like the headquarters of a firm that has been around. Software closes it plainly. The pair avoids the 'Platform Group' and 'Systems Partners' templates and reads as a real, established enterprise software firm.
Corporate.industrySummary: Mid-market enterprise software is dominated by the giant legacy vendors at the top and a long tail of point solutions at the bottom. The opening is for a structured mid-size firm focused on the operator-grade product work.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Workday (workday.com) holds the enterprise platform peer position. ServiceNow (servicenow.com) sits at the institutional tier. Procore (procore.com) does the vertical-specific middle. Atlassian (atlassian.com) holds the developer-team peer. We sit smaller, focused on the operator middle.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Enterprise software for mid-market operators that have outgrown spreadsheets and aren't ready for Workday.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Mid-market operators are too small for the giants' attention and too sophisticated for point solutions. We sit between them with operating depth and modern usability.

Creative.tagline: We caught it in code review.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Three words. Off By One is the classic programming bug: the loop that runs one too many or one too few times. The brand puts the smallest, most universal engineering mistake in the brand position. Loud, self-aware, and immediately legible to any developer.
Creative.manifesto: Most software brands sell perfection: the seamless workflow, the zero-bug release, the magical transformation. We made Off By One because the actual experience of software is debugging the small mistake nobody caught. The brand is for the engineers who know that the work is mostly in the corrections, the version increments, the patches that nobody announces.
Creative.industrySummary: SaaS branding has been polished, transformation-led, and slightly anxious. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about the actual quiet work of building good software.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Linear (linear.app) holds the design-led restraint peer. Vercel (vercel.com) sits at the modern monochrome tier. Cursor (cursor.com) does the modern dev-tool middle. Tailscale (tailscale.com) holds the warm-technical peer. We sit warmer than all of them, with a clearer point of view.
Creative.positioningStatement: A SaaS brand for engineers who know the work is mostly in the corrections.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Engineers, engineering managers, technical founders. Already use four SaaS tools. Pick tools based on whether the brand feels like the team that built it would actually use it.

dos: Quote the worst pull request title from the week
Talk like the engineer who has been on call this week
